title: IIT Madras Scientist Helps Show a Spinning Molecule Can Boost Current 100-Fold
excerpt: A helicene molecule trapped between gold electrodes rotates when voltage is applied — and its rotation opens high-conductance shapes that raise current up to 100 times, in a Nature study co-authored by IIT Madras's Anil Kumar Singh.
body:
• An international team including Dr Anil Kumar Singh of IIT Madras has shown that a single helicene molecule, suspended between two gold electrodes, can be made to rotate by applying a voltage.
  • As the molecule rotates, it passes through shapes that let electrons flow more easily, raising the current through the junction by up to about 100 times.
  • Reversing the voltage polarity reverses the rotation sequence — in all 122 cases where direction could be determined, the molecule followed the same cycle.
  • The work, published in Nature, is a proof of principle for molecular machines and switches, not a product: practical devices remain years of research away.

A single molecule shaped like a tiny screw can be made to spin by electricity — and while it spins, it lets about 100 times more current pass through it. That is the finding of an international study published in Nature involving Dr Anil Kumar Singh, an assistant professor of physics at IIT Madras, alongside researchers from Israel, Germany, Denmark and China, according to reports from IIT Madras carried by Mirror Now and Report Wire.

What rotated, in plain terms

The molecule is helicene. Picture a spring or a corkscrew shrunk to molecular size: its atoms form a spiral, like the thread of a screw. The team trapped one helicene molecule in the gap between two gold electrodes — the two metal contacts current must cross — using a technique called a mechanically controllable break junction, which creates a precise, adjustable gap and suspends the molecule inside it.

Nothing in the setup turns the molecule mechanically. The voltage itself does the work. When voltage is applied, the flow of electrons through the spiral pushes the molecule through a repeating sequence of configurations — first stepping between preferred positions, and above a threshold voltage, rotating continuously. The researchers took their cue from the Archimedean screw, the ancient device that lifts water by turning: they asked whether electrical energy and rotation could be linked in the same way inside a single molecule.

"Molecular motion could do more than simply result from electrical transport — as the molecule rotates, it accesses configurations with higher electrical conductance."

— Dr Anil Kumar Singh, IIT Madras, summarising the team's finding

Why rotation boosts the current

A molecule does not conduct equally well in every shape. As helicene rotates, some of its configurations line up in ways that let electrons move through far more readily. Rotation keeps bringing the molecule back through those high-conductance shapes, so the average current through the still-intact junction rises sharply — by up to roughly 100-fold once continuous rotation begins. Stretching or compressing the junction slightly changes the spiral's effective pitch and shifts the voltage at which the boost switches on, giving the team a second tuning knob.

Direction is controllable, too. In all 122 cases where the direction of the transitions could be determined, the molecule followed the same cyclic sequence. Reversing the voltage polarity reversed the sequence. In engineering terms, that is a motor with a reverse gear, at the scale of one molecule.

Why it matters for molecular machines

Scientists have long wanted components that work at the molecular scale — switches, motors and current modulators built from single molecules rather than etched silicon. This result matters because it shows a two-way coupling: electricity drives motion, and the motion feeds back to control electricity. A rotating molecule that changes its own conductance is, in principle, both a motor and a switch in one part.

The team and IIT Madras are explicit about the limits. This is fundamental, proof-of-principle science, not a device ready for everyday use, and significant research remains before it can be translated into technology. The plausible long-term applications named in the study are molecular-scale switches, current-modulating elements and systems for directional transport near surfaces. The next questions the researchers want to test include whether circularly polarised light or spin-polarised currents can also steer molecular motion.

For Indian science, the paper is also a marker of reach: a question about how energy, motion and momentum transfer interact at the atomic scale, answered with an IIT Madras physicist in the team and published in one of the field's leading journals.
